chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim from Abd al-Rahman from Hammad from Hariz from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

When the one in Ihram forgets and trims one of his fingernails, he gives one handful of food as charity. I said: 'And for two?' He said: 'Two handfuls.' I said: 'And for three?' He said: 'And for three?' He said: 'Three handfuls. Each nail is one handful until it becomes five. If he trims five, then upon him is one blood-expiation (dam). Whether it was five or ten or whatever it was.'

The correct interpretation of this report is to take it as indicating a type of recommendation (istihbab), because obligation (wujub) applies only to the one who trims all ten fingers. What confirms that it is a recommendation is that he said: 'When the one in Ihram forgets and trims a nail,' and the one who does this while forgetting is not bound by anything originally. Thus it is known that he meant recommendation. And that which indicates that the one who does this while forgetting is not bound by anything...

key_terms.إحرام: State of consecration for Hajj or Umrah

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for trimming fingernails while in Ihram if done forgetfully?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling in *al-Istibsar*, clarifying that the requirement of one handful of food per nail is a recommended act (istihbab) rather than a strict obligation, as the Imam specifies it applies even to the forgetful individual who incurs no penalty otherwise. This interpretation highlights the nuanced Shia jurisprudence where minor infractions in Ihram are often treated with leniency, distinguishing between the forgetful state and intentional violation. The text further notes that regardless of whether five or ten nails are trimmed, the liability remains consistent, emphasizing the proportional nature of the charity.
